newsitem.title: CHINA: ASEAN ministers converge in China to meet Sihanouk.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN ministers converge in China to meet Sihanouk.

text.p: Southeast Asian foreign ministers converged on Beijing on Wednesday to meet Cambodia's King Norodom Sihanouk for talks on the crisis in his homeland after a bloody coup earlier this month.

King Sihanouk, who reigns but does not rule in Cambodia, was holding court at his Beijing residence, meeting two officials of Group of Seven (G7) nations on Tuesday and Wednesday and accusing the police and army of Second Prime Minister Hun Sen of torturing and killing political opponents. The king met for several hours with Yukio Imagawa, a former Japanese ambassador to Cambodia, after Tokyo sought an audience to hear Sihanouk's view on the situation in Cambodia, a Japanese embassy official said.
"The talks were very private," the embassy official said, adding that the secrecy was at Sihanouk's request.
King Sihanouk on Tuesday met Claude Martin, deputy secretary general of the French Foreign Ministry, but officials refused to give details.

Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines arrived in Beijing and Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas was due later in the Chinese capital for talks with Sihanouk on Thursday.
"We have come here to listen to the king," Thailand's Prachuab Chaiyasarn said on his arrival.
The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) has mandated the three foreign ministers to meet Sihanouk to try to promote a negotiated settlement in Cambodia.
"We will listen to Sihanouk's views and suggestions on how we can help to find solutions if all parties in the dispute are willing," Alatas said in Jakarta before leaving for Beijing.

"We don't have any recipe to solve the problem...so we will listen to his views," he said. Alatas said the ASEAN ministers would convey the decision to postpone Cambodia's entry and listen to Sihanouk's views on the situation in Cambodia. Sihanouk, in a letter sent from Beijing on Tuesday to acting head of state Chea Sim in Phnom Penh, called for an end to murder and bloodshed in the conflict between the second prime minister and his son, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh, who was deposed in the coup.

"I am profoundly distressed at the reports that the military and members of the national police have cruelly tortured and killed without mercy their enemies after having arrested or captured them," Sihanouk said.

The king's message followed reports from Phnom Penh quoting western officials as saying at least 25 people have been killed in custody since Hun Sen seized power in Phnom Penh on July 6. A diplomatic source in Phnom Penh on Wedneday said the number could be as high as 40.
Some of those allegedly killed were reportedly tortured first.

Hundreds of supporters and soldiers loyal to Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party are believed to remain in detention, although officials of Hun Sen's former communist Cambodian People's Party (CPP) have disputed reported figures and denied allegations of mistreatment.

Sihanouk urged that those detained or arrested as enemies of the state be treated in line with the law, as well as in accordance with provisions of relevant international treaties to which Cambodia is a signatory state.
"If we regard the current situation in Cambodia as a state of war, we must properly abide by the Geneva Convention provisions relating to treatment of prisoners of war," he said.
Sihanouk stressed his own neutrality in the crisis.
"I take no side with my son," he said.
